The Story of Uddayan

I pay homage to the Jina, the Jina's word, and the Jain sages, and write here the story of King Uddayan, who practiced the third limb of right faith — nirvichikitsa, freedom from doubt.

Uddayan was the king of Rauravak, a city in the land of Kachchh. He was a man of right vision, generous, thoughtful, a true devotee of the Jina, and just in all his dealings. His subjects loved him dearly, and he in turn devoted himself to their welfare.

His queen was Prabhavati, a woman of great virtue and purity of heart. She spent her days in charity, worship, fasting, and the study of sacred texts.

Uddayan governed his kingdom in peace and prosperity. He performed every religious duty within his power. In short, he was happy — free from worry, and his realm was untroubled by any enemy.

The Heavenly Assembly

One day, the lord of Saudharm heaven was addressing his celestial court. He spoke of how the true gods in this world are the Arhant lords, free from hunger, thirst, disease, sorrow, fear, birth, decay, and death — beings who liberate souls from the suffering of the world. He described true dharma as marked by forgiveness, gentleness, straightforwardness, and ten such virtues. He praised the true guru as one who possesses nothing and is free from anger, pride, deceit, greed, attachment, and aversion.

"And the truest faith," he said, "is that which inspires delight in the nature of the soul. This delight — this shraddha — is what bestows heaven and liberation. It arises from loving the dharma, from pilgrimage, from celebrating the Jina's festivals, from restoring ancient temples, from consecrating images, and from cherishing fellow believers. Right faith is the supreme treasure of this world. Nothing can equal it. It alone destroys rebirth in lower states and grants heaven and liberation."

As the lord of heaven described the eight limbs of right faith, he lavished praise upon King Uddayan for his practice of nirvichikitsa — freedom from doubt and revulsion. Hearing a mortal praised so highly, a celestial being named Basav grew curious. He approached the lord of heaven and asked why this king was so distinguished.

The Test

The lord of heaven replied, "Uddayan's faith is unwavering. He has overcome all revulsion — even towards the most repulsive things — for the sake of dharma. If you wish to test this, descend to earth and try."

Basav accepted the challenge. He descended to Rauravak and took the form of a hideous, rotting corpse, lying in the king's path. The sight was so revolting that no one could bear to look at it, let alone approach it. The entire city was thrown into turmoil.

When the news reached Uddayan, he went to the spot. Others turned away in disgust, but the king, steady in his faith and free from revulsion, calmly lifted the body himself and carried it to a proper place for rites. He performed the last ceremonies with dignity and respect.

At that moment, Basav shed his disguise, revealed his celestial form, and bowed before the king. "Your Majesty," he said, "the lord of heaven praised you for your freedom from doubt and revulsion. Today I have witnessed it with my own eyes. Your faith is indeed supreme."

With these words, the deity returned to heaven. King Uddayan continued to rule with justice and compassion, his faith only deepened by the ordeal. In the fullness of time, he completed his earthly life and ascended to a heavenly abode.

The Teaching

Revulsion — the instinct to recoil from the unpleasant — is a subtle barrier to spiritual progress. Uddayan showed that true faith sees beyond the surface of things. When we overcome our aversion and act with equanimity, we honor the deepest teachings of the Jina.
